items.prose: The 12-loan tree from lesson 1. A new loan has leverage 2.6 and interest cover 1.4.
items.question: What does the tree predict?

options.text: Default: it lands in the leaf with 1 D and 0 R

options.why: You stopped after the first question. Cover 1.4 is below 1.5, which sends the loan to the default leaf.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Answer both questions on the loan's path.

explain.text: Leverage 2.6 takes the *leverage ≤ 3* branch. Cover 1.4 is at most 1.5, so the loan lands beside loan 5, a default.

items.prose: A node holds 6 defaults and 2 repaid loans.
items.question: What is its Gini impurity?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square both shares, add them and subtract from 1.

byKey.err: 0.25 is the error rate. Gini squares the shares.
byKey.sumsq: 0.625 is the sum of the squares. Gini is 1 minus it.

items.prose: A node of 20 loans, 10 D and 10 R. Split X gives (5 D, 5 R) and (5 D, 5 R). Split Y gives (9 D, 3 R) and (1 D, 7 R).
items.question: Which split does a tree choose, and what is its Gini gain?

options.text: X, because its sides are equal in size
options.why: You chose by balance. X's sides are as mixed as the parent, so it gains nothing.
0.3125 is Y's weighted child Gini. The gain is $0.5 - 0.3125$.

options.text: Either: both send 10 loans each way
options.why: Y sends 12 and 8, and both of its sides are purer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each side's Gini by its share of the 20 loans.

items.prose: A regression tree's leaf holds five days with next-day vol 14%, 15%, 18%, 15% and 23%.
items.question: What does the leaf forecast?

widget.label: Leaf forecast
widget.accept: 17: the mean of the five days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A leaf forecasts the mean of its training targets.

byKey.median: 15 is the median. The mean, 17, minimises squared error.

items.prose: A tree with `min_samples_leaf=25` is fitted to 200 training loans.
items.question: What is the largest number of leaves it can have?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every loan sits in one leaf, and each leaf holds at least 25.

byKey.twentyfive: 25 is the floor per leaf. Divide the 200 loans by it.

explain.text: Eight leaves of 25 use all 200 loans, so no tree can have more.

items.prose: An analyst splits 500 loans into 300 train and 200 test. She tries ten values of `ccp_alpha`, picks the one with the best test accuracy, 81%, and reports 81%.
items.question: What should she have done?

options.text: Choose `ccp_alpha` by cross-validation on the 300 training loans, then score the test set once
Nothing: the trees were fitted on the training loans only
options.why: The test set still chose the winner among ten trees, so its score is flattered.

options.text: Try more alphas on the test set to be sure
options.why: More tries on the test set make the winner's score more optimistic, not less.

options.text: Pick the alpha with the best training accuracy
options.why: Training accuracy always prefers the least pruning, alpha 0.

feedback.correct: Tune on the training rows; test once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which rows may help choose a setting?

explain.text: Picking the best of ten test scores leaks the test set into the choice. Cross-validate on the training rows, refit, and score the test set once.

items.prose: A regression tree forecasts a stock's realised vol from yesterday's vol. It was trained on days with yesterday's vol between 10% and 35%. Its last leaf, for yesterday's vol above 29%, has mean 31%.
items.question: What does it forecast when yesterday's vol is 70%?

widget.label: Forecast at 70%
widget.accept: 31: every value above 29 falls in the last leaf.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which leaf does 70% fall into?

byKey.seventy: A tree cannot forecast past its leaf means. 70% lands in the last leaf, which says 31%.

explain.text: Every question compares yesterday's vol with a threshold below 35%, so 70% answers like 36% would. The forecast is the last leaf's 31%.

items.prose: A node holds four days with targets 2, 4, 10 and 12. A split puts {2, 4} left and {10, 12} right.
items.question: By how much does the split lower the total squared error?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the parent's squared error around 7, then each side's around its own mean.

byKey.parent: 68 is the parent's squared error. Subtract the children's 2 + 2.
byKey.child: 4 is what is left after the split. The drop is 68 − 4.

explain.text: Parent mean 7: $25 + 9 + 9 + 25 = 68$. Left mean 3 and right mean 11 each leave $1 + 1 = 2$. The drop is $68 - 4 = 64$.

items.prose: A branch with 4 leaves has total weighted impurity 0.020. Collapsed to one leaf, its impurity would be 0.050.
items.question: At what `ccp_alpha` does pruning the branch break even?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the extra impurity by the number of leaves the cut removes.

byKey.nodiv: 0.03 is the extra impurity. The cut removes 3 leaves, so divide by 3.
byKey.four: Four leaves become one, so the cut removes 3 leaves, not 4.

explain.text: Cutting removes 3 leaves and adds 0.030 of impurity: $\alpha = 0.030 / 3 = 0.01$. Above that, the branch is pruned.

items.prose: You refit an unlimited tree on two bootstrap samples of the same 300 loans. The first tree's root asks about leverage, the second's about cover.
items.question: What is the best reading?

options.text: A deep tree has high variance: small changes in the rows change its questions
One of the fits is wrong: the data are the same
options.why: The samples differ in which rows they repeat or leave out. A deep tree magnifies such differences.

options.text: The tree has high bias, so it cannot settle on a feature
options.why: Its bias is low: it fits every training row. The instability is variance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What changed between the two fits, and how much did the tree change?

explain.text: Each bootstrap sample repeats some loans and drops others. A deep tree's questions follow those changes, so it is low bias and high variance. Averaging many such trees, in level 2, cancels much of the variance.
